title: Signs of alcohol poisoning in a friend
answer: Drinking a lot of alcohol quickly can be deadly. Danger signs include confusion, not waking up, vomiting while barely awake, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, and seizures. Call 112 straight away. While waiting, do not leave the person alone, lay them on their side so they do not choke on vomit, and keep them warm. Do not give coffee, cold showers or more drink; these do not help.

title: Alcohol and the teenage body and brain
answer: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, and alcohol can harm this growth, affecting memory, learning and mood. Young people also get drunk faster and are more likely to have accidents, fights, unplanned sex and alcohol problems later. Drinking can worsen sadness and anxiety. The safest choice for teenagers is not to drink. If you do drink as an adult, drink small amounts and never drive afterwards.

title: Alcohol and men's sexual health
answer: Many people think alcohol improves sex, but it often does the opposite. Drinking can make it harder to get or keep an erection and harder to reach climax. Heavy drinking over time can lower testosterone, reduce sperm quality and lower fertility. It also increases risky choices like sex without a condom. Cutting down usually helps these problems improve. If problems continue, see a health worker.

title: Cannabis and sexual health
answer: Cannabis (marijuana, urumogi) affects judgement and memory, so people who use it are more likely to have unplanned or unprotected sex. Regular use may lower sperm quality in men, upset periods in women, and harm the developing brain, increasing the risk of anxiety, low mood and serious mental illness in some young people. It can also become hard to stop. If you are worried about your use, talk to a health worker or call 114.

title: Drugs and sexual risk
answer: Drugs change how people think and act, which makes unprotected sex, multiple partners and sexual abuse more likely. Some people exchange sex for drugs, which carries high risks. Sharing needles or syringes to inject drugs can spread HIV and hepatitis directly through blood. If you use drugs, never share needles, always use condoms, and seek help. Health workers can test you and support you without judging.

title: Using alcohol or drugs to feel braver about sex
answer: Some young people drink or use drugs to feel less shy before sex. But if you need alcohol to feel ready, it may be a sign you are not ready yet. Being high or drunk makes it harder to choose safely, use a condom, give or understand consent, and remember what happened. Real confidence comes from feeling comfortable and respected. Take your time; there is no rush.

title: Refusing alcohol at parties
answer: You can enjoy a party without drinking. Hold a soft drink or water so fewer people offer you alcohol. Have a simple answer ready, like 'No thanks, I have to wake up early' or just 'No thanks.' Go with friends who respect your choice and plan how you will get home. If people keep pressuring you, it is okay to leave. Real friends accept your decision.

title: Getting help for alcohol or drug use
answer: If you feel you drink or use drugs too often, need more to feel the same effect, or struggle to stop, help is available. You can talk to a nurse at your health center, who can support you or refer you to a hospital service. A school counsellor or trusted adult can also help. Call 114 for free advice. Stopping is easier with support, and asking for help is a strong step.

title: Shisha smoking risks
answer: Shisha (hookah or water pipe) is not a safe alternative to cigarettes. The water does not filter out the harmful chemicals. A single session can expose you to a lot of smoke, carbon monoxide and nicotine, which is addictive. Shisha is linked to lung and heart disease, cancers and lower fertility. Sharing the mouthpiece can also spread infections. The healthiest choice is not to use it.

title: Sniffing glue and solvents
answer: Sniffing glue, fuel, paint thinner or other chemicals to get high is extremely dangerous. These fumes can damage the brain, liver, kidneys and lungs, cause memory problems, and can even cause sudden death the first time someone uses them. People who sniff solvents are also more vulnerable to abuse and risky sex. If you or a friend use them, please get help from a health worker or call 114.

title: Smoking and women's reproductive health
answer: Smoking harms women's reproductive health. It can make it harder to get pregnant, cause more painful periods, and increase the risk of cervical cancer. In pregnancy it raises the risk of miscarriage, early birth and small babies. Smoking also damages the heart and lungs and ages the skin. Women who smoke should tell their health provider when choosing contraception. Quitting at any age brings health benefits.

title: Smoking and men's sexual health
answer: Smoking damages blood vessels, including those that carry blood to the penis, so over time it can cause erection problems. It also lowers sperm quality and number, which can reduce fertility. Smoking increases the risk of heart disease and cancers, including some that affect the genitals. Many of these effects improve after quitting, so stopping early is one of the best things you can do for your sexual health.

title: Is vaping safe
answer: E-cigarettes or vapes are not safe for young people. Most contain nicotine, which is very addictive and can harm the developing brain, affecting attention, learning and mood. Vape liquids and aerosols contain chemicals that can damage the lungs. Some young people who vape later start smoking cigarettes. Sweet flavours are designed to attract youth. The healthiest choice is not to vape at all.

title: Second-hand smoke
answer: Second-hand smoke is the smoke you breathe in when people near you smoke. There is no safe level. It can cause coughing, asthma attacks, chest infections, and over time heart disease and lung cancer. It is especially harmful to babies, children and pregnant women. If family members smoke, kindly ask them to smoke outside and away from others. Open windows do not fully protect you.

title: Quitting smoking or vaping
answer: Quitting nicotine can be hard but many people succeed. Choose a quit date, tell friends and family, and remove cigarettes or vapes from your space. Notice your triggers, like stress or certain friends, and plan other things to do, such as chewing gum, walking or drinking water. Cravings usually pass in a few minutes and get weaker over time. A health worker can support you, or you can call 114.

title: Not getting an erection sometimes
answer: It is normal for young men to sometimes not get an erection or lose it, especially when tired, stressed, nervous, after drinking alcohol, or when not really in the mood. This does not mean something is wrong with your body. Erections come and go naturally. Worrying a lot can make it happen more. If it happens almost every time for several months, it is a good idea to see a health worker.

title: Morning erections
answer: Waking up with an erection is normal and healthy for boys and men. It happens naturally during sleep several times a night and is linked to the sleep cycle, not to sexual thoughts. A full bladder may also play a part. Morning erections are a sign that blood vessels and nerves are working well. There is nothing to be embarrassed about, and they usually go away on their own.

title: Performance anxiety
answer: Performance anxiety is worry about 'doing well' sexually, such as fear of losing an erection, finishing too fast, or disappointing a partner. Stress releases hormones that make erections and arousal harder, so worry can create the very problem you fear. Being with a partner you trust, going slowly, communicating, and not using alcohol help. Remember you never have to have sex to prove anything. If worry continues, a health worker can help.

title: When erection problems need a health worker
answer: If you can rarely or never get or keep an erection for a few months, or it happens suddenly with pain or after an injury, see a health worker. Ongoing erection problems can be linked to stress, depression, alcohol, smoking, drugs, some medicines, or health issues like diabetes or heart problems. A health worker can check you privately. Do not buy sex pills or herbs from markets or online; they can be dangerous.

title: Erection that will not go down
answer: An erection that lasts several hours (about four hours or more) and is painful, without sexual excitement, is called priapism. It is a medical emergency, because it can damage the penis permanently. It is more common in people with sickle cell disease and after some drugs or medicines. Go to the nearest hospital or health facility immediately or call 112. Do not wait for it to pass.

title: Early ejaculation
answer: Ejaculating sooner than you or your partner would like is very common, especially for young men and in new relationships. Nervousness and excitement play a big role, and it often improves with time, experience and feeling relaxed. Slowing down, breathing calmly and talking with your partner can help. It is not a disease and does not affect fertility. If it worries you a lot, a health worker can talk with you. Avoid creams or pills from markets.

title: Low sexual desire
answer: Sexual desire naturally goes up and down. It can be lower because of stress, tiredness, sadness, relationship problems, past bad experiences, illness, alcohol or some medicines, including some hormonal methods for some people. Having lower desire is not a disease, and nobody should pressure you. If a change in desire bothers you or comes with low mood or other symptoms, talk to a health worker.

title: Different desire levels in a couple
answer: It is very common for partners to want sex at different times or amounts. Neither person is wrong. Talk openly and kindly about how you feel, without blame. Respect is key: no one should be pushed, guilted or forced into sex, even in a relationship or marriage. Spending time together in other ways can strengthen closeness. If differences cause a lot of stress, a counsellor or health worker can help.

title: Not feeling interested in sex
answer: Some young people feel little or no interest in sex or sexual attraction, and that is okay. Everyone develops at their own pace, and some people simply feel less sexual attraction throughout life. You do not need to force yourself or follow what friends do. You can still have close, loving relationships. If lack of interest is new and comes with sadness, tiredness or other changes, talk to a health worker.

title: Pain during sex for women
answer: Sex should not be painful. Pain can happen because of nervousness, not enough arousal or wetness, infection, dryness, injury, or other conditions that need checking. Pain deep in the belly with fever or unusual discharge may be an infection. Do not ignore it or keep going through pain. Stop, talk with your partner, and see a nurse or health worker at the health center so they can find the cause and help.

title: Genital pain during or after sex for men
answer: Pain in the penis, testicles or lower belly during or after sex or ejaculation is not normal if it keeps happening. Causes can include infections, including STIs, problems with the foreskin, injury or prostate inflammation. Burning when urinating or discharge from the penis are signs to get checked soon. See a health worker at the health center; most causes can be treated. Use condoms until you are checked.

title: Vaginal dryness and lubrication
answer: The vagina naturally makes moisture when a woman feels relaxed and aroused. Dryness can happen if she is nervous, not ready, not aroused enough, after childbirth, while breastfeeding, or with some medicines or hormonal changes. Dryness can make sex uncomfortable and cause small tears. Taking time, communicating and using a suitable lubricant can help. If dryness continues or comes with itching or pain, see a health worker.

title: Choosing a lubricant with condoms
answer: If you use a lubricant with latex condoms, choose a water-based or silicone-based lubricant. Oil-based products like petroleum jelly, body lotion, cooking oil, shea butter or baby oil can weaken latex and make condoms break. Saliva is not a good lubricant and can carry infections. Some condoms already come lubricated. You can ask at a health center or pharmacy for a lubricant that is safe with condoms.

title: What an orgasm is
answer: An orgasm, or climax, is the peak of sexual pleasure, when built-up tension is released, often with a pleasant feeling and muscle contractions. Both men and women can have orgasms. In men it usually happens with ejaculation. Orgasms can happen during sex, masturbation or in sleep. Not everyone experiences them the same way, and it is normal to learn about your body over time.

title: Penis size worries
answer: Many boys and men worry their penis is too small, often because of jokes or pornography, which shows unusual sizes. Penises vary a lot in size when soft, but sizes are much more similar when erect. The penis keeps growing during puberty, often until the late teens. Size does not affect fertility, manhood or the ability to have a satisfying relationship. If you have real concerns, a health worker can check privately.

title: A curved penis
answer: It is common for an erect penis to curve a little up, down or to one side. Most penises are not perfectly straight, and a slight curve is normal and does not affect sex or fertility. See a health worker if the curve is new, getting worse, painful, if you feel a hard lump in the penis, or if it makes sex difficult.

title: Penis enlargement products
answer: Pills, creams, herbs, oils, pumps or exercises sold to make the penis bigger do not work in a safe, lasting way. Some contain hidden medicines or chemicals that can be dangerous for the heart or skin, and some cause injury, swelling or infection. Sellers profit from people's worries. Penis size is decided by genes. If you are worried, talk to a health worker instead of risking your health.

title: Testicle size worries
answer: Testicles grow during puberty and come in different sizes. It is normal for one testicle to be a little larger than the other. Size does not usually tell you about fertility or manhood. See a health worker if a testicle seems to be shrinking, one is missing from the scrotum, there is a lump or swelling, or there is pain. Steroid use can also shrink testicles.

title: Normal semen colour
answer: Healthy semen is usually whitish, grey or slightly yellowish, and it can be thick or watery. Colour and thickness can change with how often you ejaculate, how much water you drink and what you eat. See a health worker if semen is red, pink or brown (which may mean blood), green or strongly yellow with a bad smell, or if you have pain, burning or discharge, as these may be signs of infection.

title: Blood in semen
answer: Seeing blood in semen, which may look pink, red or brown, can be frightening. In young men it often has a simple cause, such as a small burst blood vessel, and may go away by itself. But it can also be caused by infection or other problems, so it is wise to see a health worker, especially if it happens more than once or comes with pain, fever, burning when urinating or blood in urine.

title: Amount of semen
answer: The amount of semen varies from person to person and from time to time. It is usually less if you ejaculate often and more after several days without ejaculating. Drinking little water can also reduce it. The amount does not show how strong or fertile you are. If you suddenly produce very little or no semen at all, or have pain, see a health worker.
